description_full: Capital One Financial Corporation operates as the financial services holding company for the Capital One, National Association, which engages in the provision of various financial products and services in the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom. It operates through three segments: Credit Card, Consumer Banking, and Commercial Banking. The company accepts checking accounts, money market deposits, negotiable order of withdrawals, savings deposits, time deposits, and sweep accounts. Its loan products include credit card and personal loans; auto and retail banking loans; and commercial and multifamily real estate, and commercial and industrial loans. The company offers credit and debit card products; bank lending; and provides advisory, capital markets, net interchange, treasury management, and depository services. It serves consumers, small businesses, and commercial clients through digital channels, branches, cafés, and other distribution channels located in New York, Louisiana, Texas, Maryland, Virginia, New Jersey, and the District of Columbia. Capital One Financial Corporation was founded in 1988 and is headquartered in McLean, Virginia.

financial_summary: Capital One Financial Corporati is a large-cap financial services business with a $117.3B market cap on $53.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +16% over the past three years and +9% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 5% against a 11% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $26.1B in free cash flow — roughly 49 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 11.30× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 6.8× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 0.2× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 4.4% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 4% operating margin trails the Financial Services median (29%) by 25pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.16x its revenue share).
It accounts for 1.3% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-16.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 514 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 7% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 25% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 31% and a beta of 1.22, it amplifies market moves.
Liquidity is deep, with about $725.1M traded a day.

val: The stock trades 53% below its DCF fair value of $418, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 47%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $287 to $604 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Financial Services peers: P/FCF 4.5 vs 13.0 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 486% above its 10-year median.
The 21 covering analysts target $255 on average, 31% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 2.3% annual cash-flow growth, 11pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 5% falls short of the cost of capital of 11.3%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.50).
It converts 49% of revenue into free cash flow.
As a lender it runs a net interest margin of 8.47% and an efficiency ratio of 51% (lean).
It earns a 2% return on equity.
hlth: CET1 capital of 13.2% sits comfortably above the ~7% regulatory minimum with buffer.
Non-performing loans are 1.49% of the book.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 16.0% over 3 years, 13.4% over 5 years and 8.6% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 8.8% on average.
Analysts expect 10.4% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.2%, and institutions hold 90%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (32 sales, net $43.0M sold).
It returns 4.4% a year to shareholders (3.2% in buybacks and 1.6% in dividends).
The share count has grown 7.8% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 30 consecutive years, raising it 26.9% a year over the last five.
people: With about 77,500 employees, each generates about $689K of revenue, 1.4x the Financial Services median, and revenue has grown 9.2% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $337K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
CEO pay is $6.8M (10x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
